doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Label, collaborations and the working artist
title: Fatherhood and Horace Tapscott as symbolic mentor
summary: Having children, Mingus's 'let my children hear music', and Horace Tapscott's ethic of art as contributive not competitive.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: Does having — speaking of young people — does having children change your work at all?

Well it’s like Charles Mingus said, “Let my children hear music.” And I just want to — well not only that but one of my friends and I guess I could say he was a mentor, maybe more of a symbolic mentor, was the late Horace Tapscott, who was the leader of the Pan African Peoples Arkestra in Los Angeles. Are you familiar with him?

You know I mean he was like a cultural warrior and a well loved person and he passed away in February 1999. But he said you know art should be contributive. Not competitive. And he stayed in Los Angeles in the hood and nurtured a lot of people. And he didn’t leave the area to go to New York to become successful. And so, and he was around the time with like the Watts riots and you’d bring music on a flatbed truck, I mean sort of a jazz mobile. I’m not quite sure of the history. I mean I’m also kind of tired so it’s probably hard for me to speak of that. Actually there’s a book that even mentions me that’s by Steven Isor called Songs of the Unsung: the Musical Journey of Horace Tapscott. It’s very inspiring. But family is important. I mean the artists that I’m around, that’s very important tradition and legacy. Because it’s not just about the artist, just the artist themselves, but these are — my experiences are important to give to my child because it gives my 8-year-old daughter something that’s very special.
